newsitem.title: USA: AT&T, Baby Bells offer plan to cut phone rates.
newsitem.headline: AT&T, Baby Bells offer plan to cut phone rates.

text.p: Long-distance giant AT&T Corp. teamed up in an unusual alliance with Bell Atlantic Corp. and Nynex Corp. to propose a plan Friday they said would cut customer phone bills $400 million a year.

AT&T and its Baby Bell rivals, seeking to break a logjam at the Federal Communications Commission, also said their proposal would slash by $2.5 billion a year the $11 billion long-distance carriers pay to access the local phone network.
The FCC is trying to develop rules by next month to reduce access charges and overhaul the system that ensures low-income and rural Americans get quality and affordable phone service.
But FCC Chairman Reed Hundt, No. 2 long-distance carrier MCI Communications Corp. and consumer advocates threw cold water on the plan, saying it would raise local phone rates.
"I don't think that Congress intended to have us raise residential basic dialtone like AT&T and Bell Atlantic proposed -- and I think I am reading Congress right on this," Hundt said in a statement.
BellSouth Corp., U S West and GTE Corp. called the proposal "astounding" and "suspect."

AT&T, Bell Atlantic and Nynex officials, however, contended phone customers would get lower rates and that schools, libraries and others would be hooked up to the Internet at discounted rates -- as stipulated by last year's telecommunications act.

"This plan meets the twin challenges of providing consumers with a price break on their telephone bills while at the same time fully funding the programs to bring the Information Age to our schools, libraries, health-care facilities, and lower-income and rural Americans," said Tom Tauke, Nynex executive vice president.
Bell Atlantic and Nynex are in the process of merging.
The carriers said their proposal would:
-- Cut by 45 percent, to 1.5 cents a minute from 2.7 cents, the fees long-distance companies pay the regional Baby Bells and other local carriers to access the local network.
AT&T reaffirmed a commitment to pass along to consumers and businesses -- dollar for dollar in the form of lower long-distance phone rates -- any cut in access charges.
-- Expand funding to ensure that basic phone service is available to high-cost rural communities and low-income areas.
-- Fund a $2.3 billion plan proposed last year by federal and state regulators to link schools and libraries to the Internet at discounted rates.

To cover the cost of hooking up schools, libraries and others to the Internet, the carriers proposed a monthly fee of 75 cents a line for all customers. This "Connect America" fee would be phased in via three 25-cent installments between July 1997 and July 1998.

The reduction in access charges would be funded by a variety of steps. Local carriers would boost the ceiling on subscriber line charges for business customers to $6 from $3.50 for a single line, and to $8 from $6 for multiple lines.
Also, a "presubscribed line charge" would be billed to long-distance carriers -- who could pass the cost on to consumers in the form of higher long-distance rates.
The charge would amount to $1 a month for residential lines and $2 a month for business lines.

"It is absolutely crazy to raise consumers' local charges $3 billion a year at a time when costs are declining and competition should be driving out inefficiencies in telephone pricing," said Gene Kimmelman, co-director of the Washington office of Consumers Union.
The $3 billion refers to the 75-cent Connect America fee and the $1 presubscribed line charge.
